questions.question: Why is the tokenizer chosen at the metric layer rather than the runner layer?
options: The tokenizer defines what counts as a token match; swapping it changes what the benchmark actually measures
Metric implementations run in O(n) time no matter which tokenizer is plugged into the metric layer
The numpy library requires a tokenizer object to be present at import time before any metric can load
Tokenizers are inherently model-specific, and the runner layer has no way to see which model produced the text
questions.explanation: BLEU and F1 are sensitive to tokenisation. Binding the tokenizer to the metric makes scores reproducible and lets you point at the rule — it is not about complexity, numpy, or model visibility.

questions.question: What does modified n-gram precision do that plain n-gram precision does not?
options: It computes the n-gram precision using a different logarithm base than the plain version does
It clips each candidate n-gram's count by the maximum count that n-gram reaches in any single reference
It runs measurably faster than plain n-gram precision because it skips repeated n-grams entirely
It returns a percentage value in the range 0 to 100 instead of a fraction in 0 to 1
questions.explanation: Clipping by the reference cap stops a candidate from inflating its score by repeating a high-precision word over and over.

questions.question: Why does BLEU use a brevity penalty?
options: Long candidates make the geometric mean used inside BLEU numerically unstable and prone to underflow
The brevity penalty exists to replace the n-gram count cap used by modified precision entirely
The brevity penalty compensates for the additive-one smoothing applied to zero-count n-gram matches
Without it, a short candidate matching a few words gets an inflated precision and unfairly high BLEU score
questions.explanation: Precision alone rewards short outputs. BP downweights candidates shorter than the reference using exp(1 - r/c) — it is not about numerical stability or smoothing.

questions.question: What does ROUGE-L compare?
options: The 4-gram precision computed against any single reference's 4-grams, same as one BLEU component
The longest common subsequence shared between the candidate and reference token sequences
The Levenshtein edit distance between the raw candidate and reference character strings
The character-level Jaccard index computed over the sets of characters in each string
questions.explanation: ROUGE-L uses the LCS length, then computes precision (LCS/cand-len) and recall (LCS/ref-len) combined with F-beta.

questions.question: Token-level F1 returns 1.0 for which case?
options: When the prediction is empty but the target string is non-empty and contains real tokens
When the prediction contains the target as a subset, plus some additional noisy extra tokens mixed in
When both the prediction and the target are empty strings, by convention treated as a perfect match
When the prediction and target happen to share exactly one overlapping token between them
questions.explanation: By convention, empty-empty is a perfect match. Any non-empty target with an empty prediction is 0.0.

questions.question: Why dispatch on metric_name rather than category in the score function?
options: It lets the same category use different metrics across tasks and keeps the dispatcher metric-agnostic
Because the category field is inherently harder for the validator to check than metric_name is
Because the string metric_name happens to be shorter to type than the string category
Because the runner layer does not actually have access to the category field at all during dispatch time
questions.explanation: metric_name is the contract. A summary task can use rouge_l on one record and bleu_4 on another; the dispatcher does not need to care.
